vignette:
The Weight of Knowing

Martin is a 68-year-old psychologist who has spent four decades helping others make sense of their inner lives. He sits in the consulting room now on the other side of the desk - a position that feels both familiar and profoundly disorienting to him. He chose a colleague in a different city deliberately, someone who would not know him from conferences or shared professional circles. Even so, he straightens his jacket before speaking, as though the habit of composure might protect him from what he is about to say.

The relationship with Elise began when Martin was 44. He had been recently divorced, his children grown, and he describes meeting her as feeling like "a second life opening up." She was charming, intellectually sharp, and intensely attentive. Within months they were living together. The first time she struck him, she had been drinking, and she wept afterward with what seemed like genuine devastation. Martin, who understood trauma responses, who understood cycles of abuse with clinical precision, told himself it was an isolated event. He did not leave for three years.

During those years, Elise hit him on at least a dozen occasions - open-handed across the face, once with a ceramic mug that left a gash above his eyebrow he told colleagues he got walking into a cabinet door. The violence was unpredictable. It could erupt over a misplaced set of keys or a dinner he had praised too enthusiastically. What Martin found most difficult to articulate, even now, is not the physical pain but the way he learned to read the atmosphere of a room the moment he entered it - the particular quality of her silence, the angle of her shoulders - scanning for danger with a vigilance that has never fully left him.

He ended the relationship after she broke two of his ribs during an argument. He told no one why they separated. He married his current wife, Ingrid, eight years later, and describes their marriage as genuinely loving and safe. And yet.

Martin still startles violently when Ingrid raises her voice, even in laughter. He finds himself frozen in doorways sometimes, taking inventory of the room before stepping in, a habit so automatic he rarely notices it until Ingrid asks why he is standing there. He has not been able to tolerate the smell of the particular wine Elise preferred; he once left a colleague's dinner party without explanation when a bottle appeared on the table. At night, the dreams come with a regularity that exhausts him - not always the same scene, but always the same quality of dread, the same sensation of being small and cornered in a body that will not move.

What brings him in now, after more than twenty years, is a moment in his own consulting room three months ago. A patient - a young man describing his abusive mother - used a phrase Elise had said to him often: You made me do this. Martin felt the floor tilt. He completed the session, he believes, professionally. Then he sat in his car in the parking structure for forty minutes, unable to identify what had just happened to him, which is perhaps the most frightening part - that he, of all people, could not name it.

He carries a particular shame that he identifies as uniquely his: he knows the literature. He has treated survivors. He understood, intellectually, why people stay, why they minimize, why they reconstruct memory to preserve dignity. He believed all of it, taught all of it, and still could not apply it to himself. This knowledge has not softened the shame so much as given it a sharper edge. He describes feeling like a fraud, though he is careful to say he does not believe his patients are fraudulent. The logic that protects others does not seem to reach him.

He looks out the window for a moment before adding, quietly, that he thinks he has been waiting twenty-four years for someone to simply believe him.
